newsitem.title: USA: Clinton takes strong lead over Dole in early vote.
newsitem.headline: Clinton takes strong lead over Dole in early vote.

text.p: Democratic President Bill Clinton surged to a strong lead over Republican Bob Dole in the first wave of major U.S. voting returns on Tuesday and seemed headed for re-election by a handy margin.

Computerized analysis of early voting returns by U.S. television networks projected Clinton the winner in Florida, Ohio, West Virginia, New Hampshire and Vermont as polls began closing in the east of the country.
Florida and Ohio were crushing losses for Dole.
Florida was a lynchpin in his long-shot strategy to pull the upset of the century over Clinton. It had not gone Democratic in a presidential election since 1976.
Ohio had been won by Clinton in 1992 but Dole hoped to take it back because no Republican has ever been elected U.S. president without taking the state.

Florida, with 25 votes, is the fourth largest prize in the electoral vote system, which determines the winner in the indirect presidential election. Florida alone provided nearly one-tenth of the 270 electoral votes required for victory.
Ohio commands 21 votes.
Clinton won 58 electoral votes to none for Dole from the first five early states.

Another bad sign for Dole was that Indiana -- one of the most Republican-leaning states in the nation -- was rated too close to call in early returns. Indiana has gone Republican in every presidential election but one since 1940.

What remained unclear early on was whether Clinton would be able to break the Republican lock on Congress even if he were re-elected -- a number of analysts said they doubted it -- and whether he would get the majority of the overall vote he covets to lay claim to a popular mandate.
He was elected in 1992 with only 43 percent support in a three-way field. This time too, Texas billionaire Ross Perot stood as a third candidate, for the Reform Party.
Interviews with voters leaving the polls suggested voters were more influenced by issues favouring Clinton than Dole -- such as economic prosperity and a compassionate image.
Clinton, the 50-year-old Arkansan who is the first president from the post-war "baby-boom" generation, is trying to become the first Democrat re-elected since Franklin Roosevelt in 1944.
Dole, 73, a former Senate majority leader from Kansas and a World War II infantryman, was trying to win the presidency back for his generation as well as his party.
But opinion polls for months have painted him as a prohibitive underdog and views expressed by voters on Tuesday suggested why.
America's current economic prosperity was sure to be a heavy influence on voters and ABC News reported that 58 percent of those leaving the polls rated the economy in good shape.
That compared with only 19 percent who thought so four years ago, when Clinton ousted Republican George Bush by hammering at discontent with a weak economy.
NBC said its exit poll also showed that 58 percent believed the country was headed in the right direction, compared to two years ago when 60 percent thought it was on the wrong track.

That was when voter discontent with the status quo threw Clinton's Democrats out of Congress by the dozen and turned control of both houses over to the Republican opposition for the first time in 40 years.

The ABC exit poll also suggested Dole's scorching attacks on Clinton's character -- virtually the whole focus of the last two weeks of his campaign -- had gained him little ground among voters who said they cared little about that issue.

A majority of Tuesday's voters said they did not consider Clinton to be honest, but that did not hurt him because, given a choice, 62 percent said it was more important to have a leader who understood their problems -- a Clinton strong point -- than to have one with good character.

Clinton and Dole each concluded the exhausting marathon of their campaigns -- the most expensive and one of the nastiest in U.S. history -- hoarse from brutal last-minute stumping and cast ballots in their respective home bases -- Clinton in Little Rock, Arkansas, and Dole in Russell, Kansas.
An odd sidelight was that, in a nation wired into the computer age and with electronic voting systems, each cast his vote on an old-fashioned paper ballot.
"I've voted before here lots ... but never voted for myself for president. I was a little nervous," Dole said after he and his wife, Elizabeth, left the polling booths.
An ebullient Clinton, seeming more upbeat than Dole, gave his 16-year-old daughter Chelsea a big hug as he emerged from the voting booth in a converted Little Rock train station.
